content:
We have already seen what the manna was. We saw how it looked, how it tasted, how it came down with the dew, how Israel gathered it, and how Yahweh faithfully fed His people every day in the wilderness. Now we come to something even greater. The manna was not only food for Israel's body.

It was also a picture; a shadow of the true bread from heaven.
Yahweh said to Moses, "Look, I'm going to rain down food from heaven for you" (Exodus 16:4). The psalmist also said, "He rained down manna for them to eat; he gave them bread from heaven. They ate the food of angels! God gave them all they could hold" (Psalm 78:24-25). So the manna was called bread from heaven. It did not come up from the ground. It did not come from Egypt.

It came down from above. Yahweh gave it to His people in a dry and empty wilderness where nothing else could sustain them.

But who is the true bread from heaven? Our Master himself answered this clearly. In John chapter six, after speaking about the manna, he said, "The true bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world" (John 6:33). Then he said plainly, "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry again" (John 6:35). The manna in the wilderness was the shadow. Christ is the true bread. Israel ate the shadow, but the true bread is the Son whom the Father sent. He said, "I am the living bread that came down from heaven" (John 6:51). The fathers ate manna in the wilderness, yet they still died. The manna sustained their bodies for a time, but it could not give them everlasting life. But Christ said, "Anyone who eats this bread will live forever" (John 6:58). This shows us the difference between the shadow and the reality. The manna came from heaven and fed Israel for the wilderness journey. But Christ came from the Father, and he gives life that reaches into the age to come.

Now let us see how the manna sustained Israel in that wilderness. There was no field to plough, no harvest to reap, and no bread to buy in that dry land. Every single day, what they needed had to come from above. If Yahweh had not fed them, they simply could not have continued the journey. And in the same way, we walk through the wilderness of this present world. What sustains us is not the wisdom of the world. What sustains us is the word of God through Christ, and the example of Christ. When our Master was tempted in the wilderness, he answered, "People do not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). He also said, "The very words I have spoken to you are spirit and life" (John 6:63).

Therefore Christ feeds us the words of God. When we are weary, his words lift us. When we are afraid, his words strengthen us. When we are tempted, his example steadies us. When we are confused, his teaching gives us light.

Peter says, "Christ suffered for you. He is your example, and you must follow in his steps" (1 Peter 2:21). So Christ is not merely the bread we hear about from a distance. He is the bread we must actually feed upon. We must receive his words, follow his steps, learn his mind, and live by the life he showed before us.

The manna was also completely sufficient for the whole journey. Israel did not need to carry supplies from Egypt. They did not need to search the desert for another kind of bread. What Yahweh gave was enough, from the first morning until the very last. In the same way, Christ is enough for our whole journey.

We do not need the wisdom of Egypt. We do not need the philosophies of men. We do not need another food for our souls. The Father has already given us everything we need through Christ and through the Scriptures. Peter says, "By his divine power, God has given us everything we need for living a godly life" (2 Peter 1:3). And Paul says, "All Scripture is inspired by God and is useful to teach us what is true. God uses it to prepare and equip his people to do every good work" (2 Timothy 3:16-17). This means the bread from heaven is a full provision. Nothing is missing in Christ. Nothing is lacking in the Word that Yahweh has given us. If we gather it, believe it, and obey it, it is enough to sustain us to the very end.

Israel ate this manna for forty years. Exodus 16:35 says, "So the people of Israel ate manna for forty years until they arrived at the land where they would settle." They did not eat it only for a short season. They did not eat it only during a feast or a difficult stretch of road. They ate it throughout the whole length of their wilderness life. In the same way, we must feed on Christ throughout our whole fleshly journey. There is no stage in the walk of the New Creation where we outgrow the bread of heaven. The young believer needs this bread. The aged servant of Yahweh still needs this bread. The one who has just begun the narrow way must gather it, and the one who has walked many years must still gather it. As long as we remain in this present body, we need the words,

the life, and the example of Christ. As long as we are in the wilderness, we must eat.
But there is something we must notice about how long this bread continued to fall. And then there is something even more striking about the day it finally stopped, after forty years of faithful provision, the manna simply did not come. Not one flake appeared on the ground, and it was never seen again. Why did Yahweh stop feeding His people? Was it because He had forgotten them, or because something far better had at last arrived? That is where we will continue tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
Our loving Father Yahweh,

We thank You for sending the true bread from heaven, Your beloved Son.

The manna fed Israel for a day, but Christ gives life that never ends.

Teach us to feed on your words through Christ, to follow his steps, and to learn his mind.

Keep us from seeking the food of Egypt when You have already given us enough in him.

Nothing is missing in Christ; let us be satisfied in the provision You have made.

"Taste and see that Yahweh is good. Oh, the joys of those who take refuge in him!" - Psalm 34:8

In the name of Christ, the living bread, we pray. Amen.
